subject: babaYagaHut
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs.
Style: Slavic folk art.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through how to design a Baba Yaga hut on chicken legs in Slavic folk art style as a diorama, keeping the scene modest with a round forest-floor base and a skull fence so the hut itself stays the clear subject.

I'm sketching the scale — hut roughly 3m wide, legs around 2m tall, total height near 5.5m — then planning a lightweight skeleton rig for the chicken legs with hip, knee, ankle, and toe joints, treating toes as digit chains. I'm laying out the foot anatomy with three forward toes and a back hallux, scaly and clawed, positioned on the floor, with thick yellow scaled legs rising from hip joints on either side of the hut body.

Now I'm working through the leg segment lengths and joint positions to make sure the IK chain can actually reach the foot target with a believable digitigrade bend, adjusting hip height and foot placement until the distances and segment lengths line up with just a slight knee bend rather than a fully straight leg.

I'm also sorting out the naming convention for the limb joints — figuring out whether a 3-segment chain with 4 points needs 3 or 4 names depending on whether a tip joint is included, matching the existing example pattern of `hipHL/kneeHL/hockHL`.

For the bend directions, I only need one per inner joint — two for a three-segment leg, so `[[0,0,1],[0,0,-1]]` covers the knee and hock. Now I'm working out the leg's hip position and overall direction, placing the hip at x=±0.9.

Thinking about rigging structure: there should be exactly one root joint, so I'll set the body joint as root at [0,2.6,0], with legs parenting from it and the toes parenting from the foot tip joint. For sweeping the legs, I'm setting radius values that taper from thigh to shank, something like [0.16, 0.1, 0.09, 0.08] across the joints, giving a feathered, tapering limb shape.

For the leg coloring I'm using a scale-pattern paint in yellow-orange tones with a darker base to mimic chicken scutes along the leg surface. For the feet, I'm placing three forward toes at spread angles plus one back toe, each built as a two-segment chain with a slight arch, keeping toe radius and height low so they rest naturally on the ground plane.

Writing claw spikes...

Then I sweep the toe chain for tapering width, and attach it to the leg chain's tip joint as parent, marking chain roles "leg" versus "digit" for the hip and toe hierarchy.

I'm working out leg side assignment using world coordinates (s=1 corresponds to the left side), then planning a feathered thigh ruff -- a ring of rust-red feather cards around the top of the leg to suggest trousers, built from a flattened puff shape at the hip.

Now I'm shifting to the hut body, the design's signature piece: a Slavic folk-art izba with carved window frames, painted floral motifs in folk red, cobalt, and yellow, a steep gabled roof with a carved horse-head ridge finial, wooden shingles, lace-trimmed eaves, a small porch, chimney smoke, and a fence topped with glowing-eyed skulls.

I'm working out the hut's proportions -- width, depth, wall height, and where it sits atop the chicken legs -- and deciding the gable faces front with a window in the pediment above the door and porch, with walls built from horizontal log construction.

Still planning log layout...

Defining wood grain function...

Now planning the hut's structure: a dark core box filling the log walls to avoid gaps, a floor platform resting on legs, and calculating wall height so I know where the roof plate sits before sketching the two sloped roof planes.

For the roof itself, I'm working out a steep gable angle around 45 degrees for an authentic Slavic hut look, pushing the total height to roughly 6.5 meters with the chimney included, then planning to texture the sloped panels with scalloped "lemekh" shingle rows.

Thinking through how to build the shingle texture, I'm weighing a stretched SVG texture map against actual geometry -- stacking overlapping scalloped strips row by row along the roof slope, each one extruded with a toothed outline to get that authentic wooden shingle silhouette.

Settling on a palette: honey wood walls, trim in red/white/blue/yellow, and dark teal-green roof shingles with moss accents, alternating row colors between two teal shades for visual rhythm. Now working out how to orient each roof row's extrusion along the slope direction so the scallop outline follows the ridge properly.

Working out the row rectangle dimensions and scallop outline, tracing the boundary counter-clockwise from the bottom-left corner through the scalloped bottom edge, up the right side, and back along the top.

I'm figuring out row overlap along the slope—since higher rows should sit outward over lower rows, I'll offset each row outward along its normal proportional to its index. Now I'm computing the roof slope length between eave and ridge coordinates.

With a half-width of 2.0 and rise of 2.0, the slope length is about 2.83, so roughly 12 shingle rows are needed, with the topmost row clipped where it crosses past the ridge line (overlapping shingles from the other side and ridge cap cover that seam).

Now I'm planning the underlayment: solid dark wood slabs beneath the shingles, built as simple extruded rectangles matching the roof outline but slightly thinner and offset lower. For the gable ends, I'm setting up triangular wall extrusions at the front and back with vertices forming the roof's peak shape.

Then I'm detailing the gables further—vertical plank siding, a round carved-frame window, and a sun rosette motif on the front gable, with pale wood coloring for the trim boards. I'm also checking that the roof's eave overhang (~2.0 along z) properly clears the walls and log ends, and adding decorative carved bargeboards along the sloped roof edges at the front and back.

Working out the lace-trim geometry...

I'm positioning the shingle strip's anchor point just beneath the roof's upper surface line, nudging the offset slightly so the strip sits flush against the underside without poking through the roof slab.

Checking eave height against wall top: at x=1.5, roof sits at y=4.95, well above the wall plate at 4.38, so there's a gable triangle filling the gap. Working out where the roof line crosses the wall top gives the gable's half-width at roughly x=2.07, which defines the triangular gable end geometry.

The eaves overhang should reveal a dark underside beneath the sloped roof plane, and I could add rafter tails or pendant details but will skip those for simplicity. I'm setting the roof depth and gable positions flush with the log faces, with bargeboards slightly outside, and placing a ridge beam log along the top at the peak.

Now I'm designing the okhlupen ridge log with a stylized horse head (konyok) carved at the front end, painted red with an eye detail, and a simple fan-shaped tail piece at the back instead of a matching head.

Sketching horse head profile outline...

Adding the throat and jaw points to close the polygon, then double-checking the vertex order traces the mane up to the ear tip and back down through the nose, muzzle, and chin without any edges crossing.

Now I'm figuring out how to place a decal eye on the lateral faces of the extruded head -- since the extrusion thickness runs along x,y, I need to compute the local-to-world normal direction to orient the eye plane correctly on each side.

For the painting style, I'm leaning toward flat bright Slavic folk-art colors with dark outlines and motifs rather than toon shading, using simple palettes and maybe SVG-based texture patterns for decorative elements. Now I'm thinking through the front facade layout, including where the door, porch, and window should go.

For access to the elevated hut, I'll build a rickety wooden ladder leaning from the porch down to the ground, with two stringers and eight rungs connecting them, capturing that classic Baba Yaga precarious-stairs feel.

Now I'm placing a centered arched door on the front wall with a painted red frame and carved sun motif header, deciding to keep windows on the side walls and a round window in the gable to avoid crowding the front face.

Next I'm working out the chicken legs' geometry, positioning them near the sides with toes reaching forward, and checking that the entry stairs clear the toe tips so there's no collision between the staircase and the legs.

Adding a flared chimney cap with low-poly icosahedron smoke puffs, plus glowing warm window light and skull eyes. Working out positions for eight skull posts along the arc, each skull built from a cranium sphere and jaw box with glowing eyes. Now designing the ground base as a low-poly disc with an earthy rim profile, making sure the hut's feet sit just above the disc's top surface.

I'm adding folk-art touches: fly agaric mushrooms with red caps and white dots scattered near the hut, and setting the ground offset so the legs' foot axis rests slightly above the disc top. For the window frames (nalichniki), I'm designing carved wood surrounds painted red and white with a pediment and side pillars, blue shutters with painted flowers, placed on each side wall, and working out spacing so door and window frames fit within the wall width without overlapping the log ends—deciding to skip front-facing windows and instead give the front wall a bold carved door frame with decorative panels.

Actually, I like the idea of making the hut look like a face: two front windows as glowing yellow "eyes" with folk shutters flanking a door as the "mouth." I'm working out exact placement and sizing so the windows and door frames fit cleanly within the front wall without clashing with the log corners.

Each window will be built from a frame outline plus a single textured glass plane carrying the drawn details -- amber glow, dark cross muntins, tiny curtains, and decorative red trim with white scalloping -- plus separate tilted shutter boxes painted blue for the open-shutter look.

I'm now planning the broader texture set: a lit window texture, floral blue shutters (possibly mirrored via flipped planes), an arched planked door with ornate hinge straps and sun motif, a sun rosette emblem for the gable, rust-red feather cards for the thigh area, and glowing spheres instead of textures for eye details.

Then I'm adding a hanging embroidered rushnyk (towel) texture with red cross-stitch trim near the door or eaves, grass/moss tuft cards scattered across the roof and ground, and a painted flower frieze band running beneath the gable.

Beyond that I'm considering small details: a chicken spur/spike at the ankle, a mushroom cap painted with red-and-white spots, and whether a skull texture is worth adding.

Now I'm tallying the total part budget across logs, roof, chimney, door, windows, ladder, legs, and skull fence components to make sure the whole piece stays within a reasonable 180–340 part range.

With the budget around 300 parts and the code targeting roughly 800 lines, I'm setting up imports from the builder SDK, pulling in geometry helpers like curves, limbs, shading, and texture utilities needed to construct the piece carefully since I can't test it live.

Setting up the builder and planning the root joint for the hut's body structure...

I realize parts without an explicit bone assignment will snap to whatever joint is nearest, which could accidentally bind hut pieces to leg or toe joints instead of the hips, so I need to explicitly specify `bone: hips` for the hut parts. For the ground, since there's only one root joint, I'm considering nesting it under hips as a child, which would be fine for a static diorama since everything moves together anyway.

Actually a cleaner setup: make "ground" the root joint at the origin, with "hips" as its child carrying the hut body, and legs parenting off hips — that way the hut can still animate independently.
